subject: Polity
description: Covers Zero hour, Starred questions, Adjournment motion, Quorum.

questions.stem: In the context of the Indian Parliament, what does the term 'Zero Hour' refer to?

options.option_text: The time immediately following the Question Hour when members can raise matters of urgent public importance without prior notice
The first hour of every parliamentary sitting dedicated exclusively to the Prime Minister's speech
The period when Parliament is prorogued by the President
A strictly regulated hour where voting on Constitutional Amendment Bills takes place

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: 'Zero Hour' is an Indian parliamentary innovation (not mentioned in the official rules of procedure). It starts immediately after the Question Hour (around 12:00 noon, hence the name 'Zero Hour'). During this time, Members of Parliament (MPs) can raise matters of urgent public importance without giving the mandatory 10 days' prior notice required during Question Hour.
DECOY BUSTING: The FIRST hour of every parliamentary sitting (11:00 AM to 12:00 noon) is the 'Question Hour', where MPs ask questions to ministers and hold the government accountable. Prorogation is the end of a session. Voting has no specific 'hour'.
EXAM INSIGHT: Because there is no prior notice, ministers are not bound to reply to issues raised during Zero Hour, making it a time of great chaos and political grandstanding.

questions.stem: During the 'Question Hour' in Parliament, what is a 'Starred Question'?

options.option_text: A question that requires an oral answer on the floor of the House, allowing members to ask supplementary questions
A question that requires a written reply, after which no supplementary questions can be asked
A question asked by a private member to another private member, rather than to a minister
A question related exclusively to matters of national security and defense

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: A Starred Question (distinguished by an asterisk mark *) is one for which an ORAL answer is desired by the member on the floor of the House. Because the minister gives the answer orally, other members can immediately ask 'supplementary questions' to cross-examine the minister on the spot.
DECOY BUSTING: 
- An 'Unstarred Question' requires a written reply. Since it's written and placed on the table, no supplementary questions can be asked. 
- A 'Short Notice Question' is asked orally on matters of urgent public importance with less than 10 days' notice.
EXAM INSIGHT: Starred questions are printed in Green ink, Unstarred in White ink, and Short Notice questions in Light Pink ink in the parliamentary lists.

questions.stem: Which motion is introduced in the Lok Sabha to draw the attention of the House to a definite matter of urgent public importance, and requires the support of 50 members to be admitted?

options.option_text: Adjournment Motion
No-Confidence Motion
Calling Attention Motion
Privilege Motion

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: The Adjournment Motion is an extraordinary procedure. If admitted, it sets aside the normal business of the House to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance (like a massive train derailment or a terrorist attack). It requires the support of 50 members to be admitted. It is considered a censure against the government, hence it is only permitted in the Lok Sabha, not in the Rajya Sabha.
DECOY BUSTING: A No-Confidence Motion is to prove the government lacks a majority. A Calling Attention Motion asks a minister to make a statement on an urgent matter, but it does not censure the government or interrupt normal business as drastically. A Privilege Motion is moved when a minister commits a breach of parliamentary privilege.
EXAM INSIGHT: The discussion on an Adjournment Motion must last for not less than two hours and thirty minutes.

questions.stem: What is the quorum required to constitute a meeting of either House of Parliament?

options.option_text: One-tenth of the total number of members of the House
One-third of the total number of members of the House
One-half of the total number of members of the House
Two-thirds of the members present and voting

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Quorum is the minimum number of members required to be present in the House before it can transact any business. According to Article 100 of the Constitution, the quorum for either House of Parliament is one-tenth (1/10th) of the total number of members of the House (including the presiding officer). 
DECOY BUSTING: This means there must be at least 55 members present in the Lok Sabha (out of 543) and 25 members present in the Rajya Sabha (out of 245). If there is no quorum, it is the duty of the Speaker/Chairman to either adjourn the House or suspend the meeting until there is a quorum.
EXAM INSIGHT: Two-thirds of members present and voting is the special majority required for passing constitutional amendment bills or impeaching the President, not for a daily quorum.

questions.stem: An 'Unstarred Question' in Parliament differs from a 'Starred Question' principally in that it —

options.option_text: is addressed only to the Prime Minister during Question Hour
receives a written reply and no supplementary question is permitted
can be asked only by opposition Members of Parliament
is listed for oral answer at the very end of Question Hour only

questions.explanation: An Unstarred Question is placed on the notice paper for a written reply; because it is not read out on the floor, there is no opportunity for supplementary questions. A Starred Question, by contrast, requires an oral answer and allows the member to ask supplementaries immediately after. Option A is wrong because Unstarred Questions can be directed to any Minister, not only the PM.

questions.stem: In Parliamentary budget procedure, the term 'Guillotine' refers to the practice of —

options.option_text: rejecting a Bill outright without sending it to a Select Committee
putting remaining Demands for Grants to vote when allotted time expires
introducing a No-Confidence Motion against the Council of Ministers
suspending a member for disorderly conduct during a sitting of the House

questions.explanation: Guillotine is the procedure by which all outstanding Demands for Grants are put to vote en masse once the time allotted for discussing the Budget expires, preventing individual scrutiny. It is not a disciplinary or confidence mechanism. Option C (No-Confidence Motion) is a common confusion because both can bring down a government indirectly, but they are entirely different procedures.

questions.stem: A 'Token Cut Motion' moved against a Demand for Grant seeks a reduction of the demand by —

options.option_text: the full amount, implying total rejection of the underlying policy
a specified sum to achieve desired economy in public expenditure
a nominal sum of Rs. 100 to draw attention to a specific grievance
fifty per cent of the demand as a symbolic protest against policy failure

questions.explanation: There are three types of Cut Motions: (1) Policy Cut — reduces demand to Re. 1, signalling disapproval of the policy; (2) Economy Cut — seeks a specified reduction to save expenditure; (3) Token Cut — moves a nominal Rs. 100 reduction to ventilate a specific grievance against the ministry. Option A describes a Policy Cut, and Option B describes an Economy Cut — both are frequent exam distractors.

questions.stem: A 'Half-Hour Discussion' in Parliament may be raised to discuss —

options.option_text: any matter of urgent public importance without giving prior notice
a matter of fact arising out of an answer already given during Question Hour
the annual Budget before it is referred to the Departmental Committee
the President's Address at the commencement of the joint Budget session

questions.explanation: Half-Hour Discussion (Rule 193 in Lok Sabha) is specifically a follow-up mechanism: it can be raised only when a member feels that a question answered in the current or recent session raises a matter of sufficient public importance that deserves elaboration. No vote takes place at the end of the discussion. Option A describes a Short Notice Question or Calling Attention, not Half-Hour Discussion.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes the effect of 'Prorogation' of Parliament on pending Bills?

options.option_text: all Bills pending in both Houses lapse immediately upon prorogation
Bills pending in Lok Sabha lapse while those only in Rajya Sabha do not
prorogation ends the session but no pending Bill lapses on that account
only Money Bills lapse on prorogation; all other Bills remain on the order paper

questions.explanation: Prorogation merely terminates a session; Bills that have not yet been passed simply carry over to the next session unaffected. It is Dissolution of Lok Sabha that causes Bills pending in Lok Sabha to lapse. Bills pending exclusively in Rajya Sabha (i.e., never transmitted to Lok Sabha) do not lapse even on dissolution. Option B is a common trap — it conflates the effects of prorogation with those of dissolution.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a 'Censure Motion' from a 'No-Confidence Motion' in the Lok Sabha?

options.option_text: a No-Confidence Motion must cite specific reasons; a Censure Motion need not
a Censure Motion automatically compels the Council of Ministers to resign if passed
a Censure Motion must state specific reasons; a No-Confidence Motion need not
a No-Confidence Motion is also movable in Rajya Sabha with adequate member support

questions.explanation: A Censure Motion must explicitly state the reasons for censuring the government or minister; if it does not, the Speaker rules it out of order. A No-Confidence Motion carries no such requirement — it is a straight vote of no-confidence needing only 50 members' signatures for admission. Option A is the classic reversal trap. Option B is also wrong: passage of a Censure Motion is a moral/political rebuke but does not constitutionally mandate resignation — only a No-Confidence Motion does.

questions.stem: A joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament under Article 108 cannot be convened to resolve a deadlock over which of the following?

options.option_text: an ordinary Bill rejected by Rajya Sabha after being passed by Lok Sabha
a Bill passed by Lok Sabha but kept pending in Rajya Sabha for over six months
a Constitutional Amendment Bill on which the two Houses are in disagreement
a Bill returned by Rajya Sabha with amendments unacceptable to Lok Sabha

questions.explanation: Article 108 expressly excludes two categories from its joint-sitting mechanism: Money Bills (governed by Article 109) and Constitutional Amendment Bills (governed by Article 368). For a Constitutional Amendment, each House must independently pass the Bill by a special majority; there is no joint-sitting escape route if one House refuses. Options A, B, and D all describe valid triggering conditions under Article 108 and are therefore valid grounds for a joint sitting.
